extracted.intended_audience: general readers, researchers and journalists interested in UK media regulation, media ethics, and the News of the World phone-hacking scandal
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia-style encyclopedic article documenting the News International / News of the World phone-hacking scandal, its investigations, legal actions, regulatory responses, and commercial/consequential fallout. Covers inquiries, arrests/charges, civil suits, corporate governance assessments, and related operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: PCC 2007 guidance on subterfuge
rubrics_metrics.description: The PCC's inquiry into phone hacking in 2007 concluded that phone message tapping should stop but that "there is a legitimate place for the use of subterfuge when there are grounds in the public interest to use it and it is not possible to obtain information through other means."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permits covert methods only when (a) there are public interest grounds and (b) information cannot be obtained by other means. Also contains an explicit prohibition against phone message tapping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information Commission recommendation to PCC
rubrics_metrics.description: The Information Commission, responsible for policing confidential databases, urged the Press Complaints Commission to issue "a clear public statement warning journalists and editors of the very real risks of committing criminal offences."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory bodies should publicly warn media practitioners about criminal risks associated with acquiring confidential information and the legal exposure of such conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thoroughness and scope of regulatory inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Sir Christopher Meyer 'promised to investigate "the entire newspaper and magazine industry of the UK to establish what is their practice' but opted not to question Andy Coulson on the grounds that he had resigned, and not to question any other journalist or editorial executive on the paper... The PCC's subsequent report failed to uncover any evidence of any phone hacking by any media organisation beyond that revealed at Goodman's trial.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective oversight inquiries should investigate industry-wide practice and question relevant individuals (including former/ex-resigned figures) rather than limit interviews; failing to do so risks producing incomplete findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence, remit and transparency of internal investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: News International engaged external firms (Burton Copeland, later Linklaters, Harbottle & Lewis) whose mandates were strictly constrained, did not waive privilege, and reviewed only selected emails; the names of selectors and selection criteria were never publicly disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Robust internal investigations should include a broad remit, transparency about scope and selection criteria, waiver of privilege where necessary to allow independent confirmation, review of all relevant communications (including emails and staff interviews), and disclosure of methods/findings to oversight bodies where appropriate. Limited mandates and non-disclosure can produce misleading conclusions (e.g., "rogue reporter" narrative).

rubrics_metrics.name: House of Commons Committee expectations for evidence and testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: The Culture, Media and Sport Committee repeatedly sought detailed information and was critical of executives for 'collective amnesia' and 'unwillingness to provide the detailed information that we sought, claims of ignorance or lack of recall and deliberate obfuscation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parliamentary/investigatory committees expect full, accurate, and detailed disclosure from witnesses; evasive testimony or withheld evidence undermines inquiries and grounds critical findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for selecting civil test cases (Justice Vos)
rubrics_metrics.description: High court judge Mr Justice Vos selected test cases that 'would enable him to decide the damages that were properly payable across a range of alleged factual situations, and make it possible for other cases to be resolved without the need for further hearings.' He added that the trial would cover issues of 'what was agreed to be done, by whom, for what purpose, over what period and who was involved.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When managing large numbers of similar claims, courts will choose representative test cases to determine legal and damages frameworks; key factual questions include what was done, actors, purpose, timeframe, and involvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settlement non-disclosure clauses and their effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Some settlements (e.g., Gordon Taylor) included non-disclosure clauses that prevented release of information that would confirm more than one journalist was involved in illegally acquiring confidential information, effectively preventing other potential litigants from learning that phone hacking was more widespread.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NDAs and settlement confidentiality can suppress disclosure of wrongdoing and impede discovery by other claimants and oversight bodies; reliance on settlements can therefore limit wider accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal categories of culpable conduct cited in scandal
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals were arrested or charged with offences including: conspiring to intercept communications, unlawful interception of communications (phone hacking), perverting the course of justice, misconduct in public office, bribery and corruption, violation of the Data Protection Act, computer hacking, handling stolen goods, obstruction of justice, and related offences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prosecutors and investigators pursue a range of statutory offences when confidential information is illegally acquired or when associated cover-ups occur; being aware of the statutory framing is central to charging and proving wrongdoing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigative priorities for police and prosecutors
rubrics_metrics.description: Renewed investigations (Operations Weeting, Tuleta, and Elveden) focused respectively on illegal interception of voicemail, computer-related intrusions, and bribery/corruption (including payments to serving police officers). The Crown Prosecution Service reviewed available evidence to determine criminality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective criminal investigations should follow seized documentary/electronic evidence, consider related offences (e.g., payments to police), and re-open dormant evidence when new disclosures surface; specialist operations may be set up with dedicated officers to examine different facets of wrongdoing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory and corporate 'fit and proper' and governance standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Ofcom concluded that James Murdoch 'repeatedly fell short of the conduct to be expected of as a chief executive and chairman' and other bodies (Commons committee) found Rupert Murdoch 'not a fit person to exercise the stewardship of major international company.' The Corporate Library graded News Corporation governance with an F.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulators and governance watchdogs assess senior executives and boards against standards of conduct, oversight, and responsiveness; failure to meet those expectations can prompt public censure, loss of confidence, and calls for removal or license/reputational consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence disclosure responsibilities to police and oversight bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that 'Scotland Yard received "very little material" from News International' and that email-selection and other disclosure choices were constrained suggest failures to provide full material to authorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organisations under investigation are expected to provide relevant material to law enforcement and oversight bodies; withholding or restricting disclosure (e.g., limited electronic folders, selective document production) undermines investigations and can trigger criticism or further inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalistic public-interest defense limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Some journalists and former staff defended hacking as justified by the public interest (e.g., Paul McMullan), but regulatory guidance and legal scrutiny distinguish legitimate public-interest journalism from criminal acquisition of communications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims of public interest do not automatically justify illegal methods; acceptable public-interest use of subterfuge is constrained by the PCC's test (public interest + no other means) and by criminal law prohibiting interception of communications.
